claim: In a NIST worked example of a 2^5 full-factorial ceramics-grinding experiment, stepwise regression plus a normal probability plot of effects converged on the same 12-term model containing all 5 main effects, six 2-factor interactions, and one 3-factor interaction.
stance_target: methodology for identifying significant effects in a factorial ANOVA
scope_conditions: NIST high performance ceramics experiment (sintered reaction-bonded silicon nitride), grinding parameters, 32 observations
quoted_support: By a combination of stepwise regression and the removal of remaining terms with a p-value larger than 0.05, we quickly arrive at a model with an intercept and 12 significant effect terms... In this case, we have arrived at the exact same 12 terms by looking at the normal probability plot as we did from the stepwise routine.

claim: The NIST handbook explicitly states that large interaction effects can obscure/mask the apparent importance of main effects.
stance_target: significant interactions change how main effects should be interpreted
scope_conditions: NIST ceramics grinding 2^5 factorial ANOVA example
quoted_support: Note that large interactions can obscure main effects.

claim: In the NIST ceramics example, 'Table Speed' plays a role in almost every significant two-factor interaction term yet is ranked as the least important main effect on its own, demonstrating that main-effect magnitude ranking can misrepresent a factor's true importance when it participates in strong interactions.
stance_target: main effects should not be interpreted in isolation when interactions are significant
scope_conditions: NIST ceramics grinding 2^5 factorial ANOVA example
quoted_support: "Table Speed" plays a role in almost every significant interaction term, but is the least important main effect on its own. Note that large interactions can obscure main effects.

claim: Re-running the factorial analysis separately at each level of the 'Direction' factor (a simple-effects-style stratified analysis) shows the model structure is not the same across levels: at Direction=longitudinal only Wheel Grit and Batch are significant with no interactions, while at Direction=transverse all main effects and interactions from the full analysis reappear -- demonstrating the two factors' effects cannot be interpreted independently of one another's level.
stance_target: a significant interaction means factor effects are not independent and must be examined at each level of the other factor (simple effects)
scope_conditions: NIST ceramics grinding 2^5 factorial ANOVA example, post-hoc analysis stratified by Direction
quoted_support: One might ask what an analysis of just the 2^4 factorial with "Direction" kept at -1 (i.e., longitudinal) would yield. This analysis turns out to have a very simple model; only "Wheel Grit" and "Batch" are significant main effects and no interactions are significant. If, on the other hand, we do an analysis of the 2^4 factorial with "Direction" kept at +1 (i.e., transverse), then we obtain a 7-parameter model with all the main effects and interactions we saw in the 2^5 analysis, except, of course, any terms involving "Direction".

claim: The NIST handbook notes that some analysts prefer to retain a main-effect term in the model when it participates in several significant interactions, even if that main effect is not itself statistically significant, reflecting the hierarchy principle in factorial model-building.
stance_target: model-building convention for main effects involved in significant interactions
scope_conditions: NIST ceramics grinding 2^5 factorial ANOVA example
quoted_support: Some analysts prefer to include a main effect term when it has several significant interactions even if the main effect term itself does not appear to be significant.

claim: An interaction plot in the NIST example shows two lines crossing (for Rate * Speed), which the handbook states indicates interaction between the two factors, whereas parallel lines would indicate no interaction.
scope_conditions: NIST ceramics grinding 2^5 factorial ANOVA example
quoted_support: The two lines in the r*s plot cross, indicating that there is interaction between rate and speed. Parallel lines indicate that there is no interaction between the two factors.
